title: Spectral Topology and Non-Bloch Band Theory for Domain-Wall Systems
authors: Mingtao Xu, Rui Wang, Tian-Shu Deng, Wei Yi
abstract: We study the spectral topology of one-dimensional non-Hermitian models in a domain-wall configuration, where different domains are arranged in a ring geometry. While eigenstates can localize near an interface under the non-Hermitian skin effect, we show that the localization of an eigenstate originates from the difference in the spectral winding numbers, with respect to the corresponding eigenenergy, between the two adjacent domains. We then obtain the conditions for the generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ) in the complex momentum space, by extending the Ronkin-function formalism to the domain-wall configuration. In addition to the conventional skin modes that correspond to standing waves on individual domains under the open boundary condition, a unique type of traveling-wave-like skin modes emerges, whose construction involves all domains. Besides their difference in the spatial profiles, these two types of modes obey distinct GBZ conditions, making them differentiable on the GBZ. Interestingly, the traveling-wave-like modes further carry a finite flux spectral winding number, indicating their boundary sensitivity.
summary: This paper develops a topological theory for non-Hermitian models arranged in a ring of domains (DW ring). It shows that the system supports two distinct types of skin modes—standing and traveling—whose existence is dictated by spectral winding number mismatches between adjacent domains. The methodology extends established band theories using constrained Ronkin functions to map out the generalized Brillouin zone for these complex boundary conditions.
main_problem: The study investigates the spectral topology and non-Bloch band theory for one-dimensional non-Hermitian models arranged in a domain-wall (DW) ring configuration.
main_result: The system supports two distinct types of skin modes—standing-wave-like and traveling-wave-like—whose existence and properties are governed by different topological constraints derived from spectral winding numbers. The unique traveling-wave modes carry a finite flux spectral winding number, indicating boundary sensitivity.
method: The authors extend the Ronkin-function formalism to the DW ring geometry and utilize spectral winding numbers ($\Delta_\alpha(E)$) to characterize topological protection and determine the Generalized Brillouin Zone (GBZ).
model_or_system: The model is a general one-dimensional non-Hermitian system composed of $n$ domains connected in a ring geometry ($n$-DW ring), where the DW boundary generalizes both OBC and PBC.
key_observables: Spectral winding numbers ($\Delta_\alpha(E)$), Generalized Brillouin Zone (GBZ) conditions, standing-wave-like skin modes, traveling-wave-like skin modes, and Flux Spectral Winding Number ($	ext{WDW}$).
important_parameters: The number of domains ($n$), the energy $E$, and the complex momentum parameters $\mu_\alpha$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on extending established formalisms (like Ronkin functions) to the DW ring structure, and comparisons between open chain and closed ring geometries are made in the thermodynamic limit.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic diagrams comparing mode profiles for different types of skin modes; one figure shows the topological origin using a 3-DW model by mapping winding number mismatches ($\Delta_\alpha > 0$); another compares DOS calculated via Ronkin minimum versus real-space diagonalization for the DW ring.
paper_structure: The paper develops theory by first defining spectral topology using relative winding numbers, then extends the Ronkin function formalism to derive GBZ conditions distinguishing between standing-wave (Case I) and traveling-wave (Case II) modes. It concludes by comparing the results for the closed ring versus open chain geometries.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous topological framework for understanding localization in complex, non-Hermitian structures like domain walls, which is highly relevant to engineered quantum systems where boundary effects are crucial.
